When something hits, presses, or impacts a surface with enough force to cause hidden damage — damage that you can feel or see, but that doesn't break the outer layer open — that action is called bruising. Think of it as injuring something from the inside, while the surface stays closed.
Sense 1 — To injure a body part by blunt impact

This is the most common and important meaning. When you knock part of your body against something hard — say, you bump your shin against a table — the tiny blood vessels just beneath your skin get crushed and start to leak blood into the surrounding tissue. The skin itself doesn't break or bleed outward, but a dark patch (usually red, purple, blue, or yellowish) appears under it. The action that caused this is described using the verb bruise.

"She bruised her knee when she tripped on the stairs."

"He bruised his arm after the fall."

Notice that the verb here is transitive — one thing is doing the bruising, and a body part is receiving it. But bruise can also be used intransitively, meaning you can say that a person or body part bruises without specifying what caused it:

"She bruises easily." (meaning her skin develops bruise marks with very little force)

"Fair-skinned people tend to bruise more visibly."

You can also bruise things that aren't soft tissue — bones, for example. A bruised rib means the bone was hit hard enough to damage it internally, but it wasn't cracked or broken.
Sense 2 — To damage the surface of soft objects, especially fruit

This sense works exactly like the physical body sense, just applied to objects. When a soft fruit like a peach, banana, or apple gets knocked, dropped, or pressed against something hard, the outer skin stays intact but the flesh just beneath it gets crushed and discoloured — it turns soft, dark, and mushy in that spot. That is bruising.

"The mangoes got bruised in the bag during transport."

"Handle the peaches carefully so you don't bruise them."

"These tomatoes are bruised — they won't last long."
Sense 3 — To hurt someone emotionally or damage their confidence

The verb bruise is also used figuratively to describe emotional or psychological harm. Just like a physical bruise is damage beneath the surface that isn't always immediately visible, emotional bruising refers to a kind of hurt that goes deep but isn't always obvious to others. It often involves a person's feelings, pride, ego, or self-esteem.

"His cold rejection bruised her feelings."

"Losing the competition bruised his ego."

"Years of criticism had bruised her confidence."

Notice something important here: this sense implies a moderate kind of emotional hurt — deeper than a slight sting, but not completely devastating. It suggests damage, not total destruction. You wouldn't typically say someone's spirit was "bruised" if they were utterly broken — you'd use stronger words for that.
Sense 4 — To crush or press lightly (especially in cooking)

This is a more specialised but legitimate use of the verb. In cooking, when you bruise an ingredient like lemongrass, garlic, ginger, or a herb, you press or lightly crush it — usually with the flat side of a knife, a pestle, or the back of a spoon — just enough to break its fibers slightly and release its oils, juices, or aroma. You're not grinding it to a paste; you're doing something gentler. The ingredient remains mostly intact but is just damaged enough to release its flavour.

"Bruise the garlic cloves before adding them to the pan."

"Bruise the lemongrass stalks to release their fragrance."
The One Thread Running Through All Senses

Every use of bruise as a verb carries the same underlying logic: the outer layer stays whole, but damage happens beneath it or within it. Whether it's your skin, a fruit's peel, a person's dignity, or an herb's fibers — bruising is always about impact or pressure causing internal or hidden damage without an outright break or rupture. That is what makes it distinct from words like cut, tear, or shatter, all of which involve something being broken open or apart.

These are common word combinations you'll frequently encounter with this verb:

"Badly bruised" — seriously injured or hurt (physically or emotionally).
"Bruised and battered" — a common phrase describing something or someone that has taken a lot of damage over time.
"Bruised ego/pride" — the figurative use, referring to wounded self-esteem.
"Bruise easily" — to be prone to bruising, either physically or emotionally.

To bruise means to cause injury, damage, or harm to something (a body part, an object, a feeling, or an ingredient) through pressure, impact, or force, in a way where the surface stays unbroken but the inside is damaged. It works literally on bodies and soft objects, figuratively on emotions and pride, and specifically in cooking to mean a gentle crush that releases flavour.
